API vs Event-Driven vs Batch Integration: Which Should You Choose?

Choose the connection from the workflow’s response needs, freshness limits, failure rules, and operating budget.

Published by NMITPublished 17 September 202610 min read
On this page
  1. What the three choices mean
  2. Compare the tradeoffs
  3. When an API fits
  4. When events fit
  5. When batch fits
  6. A practical hybrid example
  7. Ordering and recovery
  8. Compare operating cost
  9. Questions before choosing
  10. Common questions

Bring the workflow, its owners, and a clear definition of completion.

API vs event-driven integration is a choice about how applications coordinate a workflow. A synchronous API asks another system for a result now. An event-driven flow publishes a change for consumers to process independently. Batch integration transfers a defined collection of records in a scheduled or bounded run.

Choose an API when a caller needs an authoritative result before continuing. Choose events when consumers can react independently and tolerate a measured delay. Choose batch when grouped transfer and processing windows fit the business requirement. A system can use all three for different steps.

This comparison focuses on latency, coupling, ordering, and operating cost. It is a decision framework, not a performance benchmark. If you are still deciding which existing applications to retain, start with NMIT’s legacy system integration guide.

Define the choices before comparing them

An API is an interface, not necessarily a synchronous architecture. An HTTP endpoint can accept work asynchronously; an event producer or batch loader can also use APIs. For this guide, “API integration” means synchronous request–response unless stated otherwise.

An event describes something that happened, such as an approved order changing state. A command asks a specific recipient to do something. Sending a payment command through a queue changes delivery mechanics; it does not make that command an established payment fact.

Microsoft’s event-driven architecture guide (opens in a new tab) describes producers, channels, consumers, and the operating tradeoffs of asynchronous processing. The AWS Batch overview (opens in a new tab) describes managed batch-job execution. A job service does not define your business dataset: distinguish incremental batches from complete snapshots in the integration contract.

Also distinguish an HTTP 202 acceptance from completion. The asynchronous request–reply pattern (opens in a new tab) uses a way for callers to check progress after acceptance. If a vendor offers that flow, assess it as asynchronous work rather than assuming a successful initial response means the business task finished.

Decision table: latency, coupling, ordering, and cost

Use the table to shortlist a pattern, then verify the actual endpoint, broker, dataset, and team capabilities. “Near real time” is not a contractual delay bound; a queue can accumulate hours of work during an outage.

Qualitative comparison; actual behavior depends on implementation
Decision factorSynchronous APIEvent-drivenBatch
Latency / freshnessA result in the caller’s request window; bounded by dependenciesOften low delay, but backlog and consumers determine freshnessSchedule, transfer, and processing window determine freshness
CouplingCaller and dependency must coordinate availability and contractLess runtime coupling; schema and meaning still sharedShared file/schema, schedule, and completion agreement
OrderingConcurrent requests do not imply business orderScope ordering by entity, partition, or message groupDefine file/record order and precedence against live updates
Failure recoveryTimeout can leave a write outcome unknownDuplicate-safe processing, checkpoints, and controlled replayPartial-run accounting, restart points, and duplicate-safe imports
Operating costRequest load, rate limits, availability, and request tracingBroker, storage, retention, consumers, lag monitoring, and replayScheduled compute, data movement, validation, and exception handling
Useful workflowCurrent eligibility or order validation before proceedingDistributing approved changes to independent consumersHistorical load, scheduled reporting, and bulk reconciliation
Compare requirements, not labels

A simple request–response flow may be the right choice. Adding a broker increases responsibilities as well as flexibility. Batch can be appropriate when the business accepts its processing window and the recovery plan is explicit.

Choose a synchronous API for a result the caller needs now

Use a request–response interaction for an authoritative check that must complete before a user proceeds: checking account eligibility, validating an order, or reserving an available resource. Define the response contract, permissions, deadlines, and what the caller shows when the dependency is unavailable.

OpenAPI (opens in a new tab) describes HTTP interfaces in a machine-readable contract. Verify business meaning alongside the schema: a field named available may refer to stock at a particular warehouse or a snapshot taken earlier.

A chain of calls can couple the user experience to several downstream systems. Measure the end-to-end path and test the slowest dependency. Caching can help read workflows when the application exposes freshness and the business accepts stale answers. It cannot make an unconfirmed payment safe to repeat.

HTTP idempotent-method semantics (opens in a new tab) describe protocol behavior. A business write still needs endpoint-specific duplicate prevention and recovery. Our payment API timeout and retry guide follows the consequences of a lost response.

Before approving the approach, ask whether a temporary failure should block the user, return a pending operation, or use an explicitly approved fallback. Record that decision in the contract and acceptance tests.

Choose events for independent reactions to an approved change

Events suit workflows where one approved change feeds several applications, such as an order update that refreshes the CRM, an analytics view, and a customer notification. The producer should not need to wait for every consumer before completing its own local work.

Decoupling runtime availability does not remove shared meaning. Agree the event type, entity ID, source, schema version, occurrence time, and relevant business version. Avoid broadcasting personal or financial data to consumers that do not need it.

AsyncAPI documents (opens in a new tab) describe message interfaces and channels. Use that contract to communicate expected messages and security requirements, while defining retention, replay permission, and operating ownership separately.

When you control the source application, a transactional outbox (opens in a new tab) can persist a change and its outgoing event record together. The relay and consumer can still encounter retries, so guard downstream effects independently.

Set a freshness objective for each consumer rather than claiming every view is current immediately. A customer-facing screen may need to show “updating” or perform an authoritative read. The ERP–CRM update-frequency guide gives examples of matching data freshness to the business consequence.

Choose batch for grouped work with an accepted processing window

Batch suits historical imports, scheduled exports, independent reconciliation, and partner interfaces that provide files rather than events. It can also reduce repeated API calls when a supported bulk interface is available. The business must accept the time between a change and the next completed run.

Define each dataset with a batch ID, schema version, record count, source window, timezone, and completeness indicator. Include a checksum or equivalent transport-integrity check where supported. Know whether the file is a snapshot, a delta, or an adjustment to an earlier delivery.

Plan for a file that arrives late, a run that succeeds on only half the rows, and a duplicate file sent after an uncertain acknowledgement. Persist per-record outcomes or safe chunks, and ensure a restarted job does not repeat business effects. An overall job exit code is insufficient when rejected rows disappear from view.

Specify the handling of a missing file separately from an empty but valid file. Check duplicates, invalid identities, and totals by relevant currency or business unit. Never treat a missing record in an incremental file as an instruction to delete it.

See payment reconciliation for how grouped external records can check an operational flow independently. See ERP–CRM backfill and cutover for keeping older bulk data from overwriting live changes.

Worked example: one order journey, three integration patterns

Consider a fictional business taking a partner order against an ERP account. The following architecture is an option to test, not a deployed NMIT case study or a prescription for every business.

  1. Validate through an API: the order service asks the authoritative system whether the account is eligible. A dependency outage produces a clear pending or unavailable response rather than a fabricated approval.
  2. Record the accepted order: commit the local order and, where supported, an outgoing approved-order event record together. The event is a fact about that local commit, not proof that all applications have updated.
  3. Distribute through events: CRM and notification consumers process the approved change with separate duplicate guards. CRM delay does not require creating the original order again.
  4. Check through batch: an agreed comparison matches accepted orders with ERP records. It raises unmatched identities and incomplete downstream writes for investigation.

This design gives a buyer concrete questions: who owns the eligibility answer, what makes an order approved, how long can the CRM lag, and who resolves the comparison exceptions? NMIT’s API integration and cloud services provide the delivery context for those boundaries.

Make ordering and duplicate handling explicit

Sending messages in sequence does not guarantee that every consumer applies them in sequence. Concurrent workers, retries, and delayed older messages can change processing order. Choose the ordering scope from the business entity: updates for one order may need sequence, while unrelated orders can proceed independently.

Amazon SQS standard queues (opens in a new tab) document at-least-once delivery. SQS FIFO processing (opens in a new tab) describes ordering by message group. A broker’s duplicate or ordering feature does not guarantee that a remote database or payment endpoint performs exactly one business effect.

Store consumed event identity and the resulting local change atomically where possible. If processing calls another system, use that system’s safe operation mechanism or an explicit outcome-resolution process. Preserve the latest applied source version so an older event cannot silently regress an entity.

Distinguish work sharing from fan-out. The competing consumers pattern (opens in a new tab) spreads work among workers; a publish–subscribe design sends changes to independent subscriber groups. Adding more workers to one group does not create a new independent business subscriber.

For repeated failures, use a controlled exception path such as the SQS dead-letter queue mechanism (opens in a new tab). Investigate before replay, assess the impact on ordering, and decide whether an old message is still valid for the entity’s current state.

Estimate total operating cost, including recovery

For a quote-ready brief and supplier comparison, see our API integration project cost guide.

Do not compare only request pricing, broker charges, or the cost of one scheduled job. Include engineering, environment setup, data retention, monitoring, on-call time, reconciliation, and the business cost of delayed or incorrect records.

Build a workload model using expected records, peak rates, payload sizes, consumer count, retention days, and acceptable backlog recovery time. Add retry amplification, backfill traffic, and downstream quotas. These inputs should come from the business and measured prototypes rather than invented industry averages.

APIs require enough available capacity for the request window. Events add broker and consumer operations but let consumers absorb work independently. Batch can use bounded compute windows while creating deadlines around delivery and completion. None is always cheapest.

OpenTelemetry’s signals (opens in a new tab) can support tracing and monitoring across the chosen boundaries. Track end-to-end business completion and exception age, not just the health of the connector or queue.

Ask these questions before approving an integration approach

  • Does the caller need a result immediately, or can it receive a pending operation?
  • What is the maximum accepted stale-data window for each consuming team?
  • Which application owns the decision and the fields involved?
  • What are the actual duplicate, ordering, retention, and replay guarantees?
  • How will a partial write or an unknown remote outcome be resolved?
  • Can the team operate the selected infrastructure and recover from a backlog?
  • Who approves corrections, schema changes, and the eventual handover?
  • What representative workload will validate latency, capacity, and operating cost?

Record the answers in a one-workflow decision document. Compare the simplest viable option against alternatives, then pilot with failure scenarios. Use NMIT’s integration workshop enquiry to discuss the interfaces and operating scope.

Common questions about integration patterns

Are events always faster than APIs?

No. Events can remove a caller’s wait for downstream consumers, but business completion still depends on queue delay and processing. Measure the time to the outcome the user actually needs.

Is batch integration outdated?

No. Batch is useful for accepted processing windows, historical transfers, and independent reconciliation. It needs explicit completeness, restart, and exception rules.

Can APIs, events, and batch be combined?

Yes. A workflow can validate through an API, publish an approved change as an event, and compare external records through a scheduled batch. Each boundary needs a defined contract and owner.

ERP–CRM Integration: Data Mapping, Synchronization, and Error Handling

Agree which system owns each field, how quickly updates must arrive, and who fixes the records that fail to synchronize.

Published by NMITPublished 17 September 202610 min read
On this page
  1. Assign field ownership
  2. Match records safely
  3. Write the mapping contract
  4. Choose update frequency
  5. Resolve conflicting updates
  6. Recover failed syncs
  7. Backfill and cut over
  8. Own the running workflow
  9. Common questions

Bring the workflow, its owners, and a clear definition of completion.

ERP–CRM integration exchanges selected data between enterprise resource planning and customer relationship management systems. It lets sales teams see approved operational information and lets finance or fulfilment receive validated customer and order details.

The implementation is rarely just a field-name translation. Two records can describe the same organisation with different identifiers, different addresses, and different update times. A failed synchronization can also leave a valid order missing from one application even though the other accepted it.

This guide covers data mapping, synchronization frequency, conflicting records, and error handling. Its example is a fictional account-to-order workflow. For integrating a larger landscape without replacing useful applications, see our legacy system integration guide.

Assign authority by field, not just by application

Write a field-ownership register before enabling bidirectional synchronization. “Both systems own the customer” leaves important questions unanswered: can a sales representative change a legal billing name, and can an ERP update overwrite the sales contact’s email?

A useful boundary is one authorised writer for each field in a given business state. Other systems may display or propose changes to that field. Ownership can change at a defined lifecycle transition, but the transition needs approval and a documented rule.

Proposed ownership for a fictional account workflow
FieldAuthoritative sourceReceiving-system rule
Legal billing name / tax identifierERP, after finance validationCRM displays approved values; changes become requests
Account contact / relationship notesCRMERP receives only contact data required for operations
Credit limit / balanceERPCRM displays a timestamped, read-only view
Opportunity stageCRMDo not map directly to invoice or payment status
Accepted order statusERP after order validationCRM displays fulfilment status without editing it

Record the business owner as well as the application team. Finance approves billing-field rules; sales operations approves contact rules; integration engineering implements the contract. The exact division is organisation-specific.

Microsoft’s anti-corruption layer pattern (opens in a new tab) describes translating between systems with different semantics. Use the boundary to preserve meanings instead of forcing the ERP’s entire data model into the CRM. Our API integration services start with these interfaces and responsibilities.

Use stable keys to identify the same business entity

A name, telephone number, or email address can change. Two employees can share a company domain, and two legal entities can have similar trading names. Avoid treating those values as sufficient evidence for an automatic company merge.

Maintain a cross-reference such as ERP account 00482 ↔ CRM company 9017. Include tenant, entity type, and source system in the key. Store whether the match was supplied by an authoritative process, approved manually, or inferred and still awaiting review.

Dataverse alternate keys (opens in a new tab) offer an integration-friendly way to reference records. HubSpot’s contact API documentation (opens in a new tab) distinguishes record identifiers and supported contact operations. These are product-specific examples; check the actual object and endpoint you use.

If two CRM records map to one ERP account, quarantine the collision. Let a data steward decide whether they are duplicates, separate contacts, or separate legal entities. Preserve historical identifiers when an approved merge occurs so older events and invoices still resolve correctly.

A missing match is a visible state

Do not invent an ERP identifier to keep a sync green. An unmatched record needs a reason, an owner, and a next action. It may be waiting for legitimate finance approval.

Specify transformations, missing values, and write behavior

A mapping contract should be executable and reviewable. For every field, record the source, destination, type, transformation, requiredness, null handling, authority, and rejection reason. Keep sample records and expected results alongside the contract.

Illustrative mapping rules, not vendor schemas
Source → destinationTransformationFailure rule
CUST_NO → externalAccountIdString; preserve leading zeros and source scopeMissing key becomes an identity exception
CREDIT_STATUS → creditStatusExplicit lookup: approved, held, or unknownUnknown code is quarantined, not assumed approved
BILLING_COUNTRY → billingCountryValidate against the agreed code listReject unsupported values with a correction request
BALANCE_AMOUNT + CURRENCY → balance viewPreserve decimal precision and currency; show freshnessReject invalid precision or missing currency
CONTACT_EMAIL → operationalContactCopy only under the agreed business and permission rulesInvalid format becomes a field exception

Distinguish “field not sent” from “explicitly clear this field.” A partial update should not blank fields that the sender did not own or provide. Define how your API, file format, and mapping language represent that difference.

The OpenAPI specification (opens in a new tab) can describe HTTP payloads and response contracts. Use that description with business validation tests; a syntactically valid string may still contain an invalid account reference.

Where supported, an upsert combines create-or-update behavior around a stable key. Dataverse’s upsert reference (opens in a new tab) explains its operation semantics and table-specific differences. An upsert does not settle who owns a field or make an unrelated side effect safe to repeat.

Choose frequency from the consequence of stale data

Ask what the consuming team can tolerate before selecting events or a schedule. A credit decision before accepting an order may require a current authoritative check. A salesperson’s account summary may tolerate a timestamped cached value. A monthly historical export can usually wait for a scheduled window.

A proposed service objective might be “approved address changes appear within ten minutes during business hours.” That is an example to negotiate, not an industry benchmark. Include downtime, backlog recovery, peak volume, and downstream rate limits in the agreement.

  • Request–response API: useful when a user needs a current answer before proceeding; dependency outages affect the immediate workflow.
  • Events or change feeds: useful for incremental updates; plan for duplicates, gaps, delay, and supported retention.
  • Scheduled delta synchronization: useful when moderate lag is acceptable; preserve a durable cursor and process all pages.
  • Batch snapshots: useful for bulk comparison and history; define the snapshot boundary and its effect on live updates.

Dataverse change tracking (opens in a new tab) supports synchronizing changes with external systems under documented table and retention conditions. Do not assume an expired cursor can resume without recovery. Our API vs event-driven vs batch decision guide compares these options in more detail.

A changed-since timestamp poll needs special care around ties, clock differences, paging, and deletes. Where a reliable vendor cursor exists, prefer it. Otherwise use an overlap window, stable tie-breaking, deduplication, and a separate reconciliation process to detect missed records.

Resolve conflicts without silently choosing the newest timestamp

Suppose a sales representative edits company 9017’s display name at 10:05, while finance approves account 00482’s billing name at 10:06. The timestamps do not prove the fields have the same meaning. Apply the finance-approved billing name to the billing view and retain the sales-owned display name separately.

For the same owned field, use source versions or supported conditional writes to detect a stale update. Dataverse conditional operations (opens in a new tab) use ETags and preconditions to detect version conflicts. A rejected precondition should trigger a re-read and a decision, not an unconditional overwrite.

Do not compare version tokens from different systems as if they share a sequence. Track a source’s version in its own scope. If ordering cannot be established reliably, retrieve current authoritative state before applying a delayed notification.

For bidirectional flows, record the origin and version of changes so the receiving system’s write does not bounce endlessly back to the sender. Apply only meaningful field changes. Do not discard all integration-originated updates if that would also hide legitimate downstream business rules.

Payment status deserves a separate authority rule: a CRM edit must not manufacture a paid invoice. See payment reconciliation and financial-record ownership for that boundary.

Separate temporary failures from records that need correction

A service outage, an invalid country code, a missing parent account, and a conflicting version need different recovery paths. Store the source ID, mapping version, attempt ID, classified failure, and last successful checkpoint. Operators should see the business record involved without reading raw personal data in logs.

A proposed failed-sync policy
Failure classRecovery pathOwner
Throttling / temporary outageBounded retry; honour server timing; preserve checkpointIntegration operations
Invalid mapping / required fieldQuarantine until source data or mapping is correctedData steward and mapping owner
Missing parent recordResolve parent; retry dependent record with a limitIntegration operations and source owner
Version conflictRe-read; apply field authority or seek approvalBusiness field owner
Unknown write outcomeRetrieve destination state before unsafe replayIntegration operations

Dataverse service-protection limits (opens in a new tab) document throttling and Retry-After behavior. Coordinate worker concurrency and SDK retries so recovery does not overwhelm the target.

Amazon SQS dead-letter queues (opens in a new tab) illustrate isolating messages that repeatedly fail. A quarantine store still needs an operator, retention rules, and a controlled replay procedure. Fix the underlying reason before returning the same record to processing.

Advance checkpoints only when outcomes are durably accounted for. Depending on the feed, that can mean a successful write or a durable exception ready for later recovery. A process that reports “completed” after dropping failed rows creates data loss disguised as progress.

Backfill without overwriting newer live updates

Choose a snapshot or change-feed boundary, load historical records, and then catch up changes from that boundary. If the source cannot provide a consistent snapshot, document the limitation and use comparison passes to resolve gaps. Coordinate parent and child entities before importing dependent records.

Store source versions with imported records so an older backfill cannot overwrite a later live update. For event publishing you control, the transactional outbox pattern (opens in a new tab) connects a database change and its outgoing event record within one transaction. It does not fix a vendor feed you cannot change or remove the need for duplicate-safe consumers.

Pilot one entity type or account group. Compare key counts, sampled field values, unmatched identities, and exception ageing. Counts alone can match while the wrong records are linked. Test approved merges, deletions, explicit field clears, a stopped worker, and a restart from the checkpoint.

For dependencies across a cloud boundary, follow the hybrid cloud migration checklist before scheduling cutover.

Rollback needs a write policy and an in-flight recovery plan. Disabling the connector will not undo changes already applied. The phased legacy-integration rollout describes validation gates and the limits of reversing traffic.

Name the teams that own freshness and correctness

Monitor freshness lag, oldest unprocessed change, cursor age, failed records by class, and identity collisions. Distinguish the backlog caused by a dependency outage from the quarantine caused by invalid data. Track per-entity success instead of only a connector uptime percentage.

OpenTelemetry signals (opens in a new tab) provide a vocabulary for traces, metrics, and logs. Correlate an incoming source change with its transformation and destination write, while restricting payload visibility and avoiding personal data in metric labels.

Give each exception category a named team and a correction path. Agree who approves mapping changes, who handles after-hours outages, and who checks downstream business rules after a replay. Review contracts when either application changes schema or permissions.

The delivery is complete when the receiving team can explain a delayed update and recover a failed record. Discuss the initial scope through NMIT’s API integration enquiry, then agree the operating handover with our integration and DevOps teams.

Common questions about ERP–CRM integration

Should every customer field sync in both directions?

No. Decide who owns each field and which changes the other application can propose. Unrestricted bidirectional writes create conflicts and feedback loops.

How often should ERP and CRM synchronize?

Use the business consequence of stale data to set a freshness objective. A current credit check, a customer summary, and a historical export can require different patterns and schedules.

What should happen when one record fails?

Persist its reason and recovery state. Retry temporary failures within bounds, quarantine invalid data, and resolve conflicts through the field owner. Do not discard the row to advance the job.

Legacy System Integration: Connect ERP, CRM, and Partner Systems Without a Full Rewrite

Keep the systems that work. Give them clear contracts, reliable connections, and an owner for every workflow.

Published by NMIT17 September 202612 min read
On this page
  1. Integrate or replace?
  2. Map the current landscape
  3. Choose the right pattern
  4. Define ownership and contracts
  5. Plan for partial failure
  6. Secure each boundary
  7. An ERP–CRM–partner example
  8. Roll out in controlled phases
  9. Own the production workflow
  10. Readiness checklist
  11. Common questions

Legacy system integration connects existing applications with other business systems without immediately replacing their core functionality. An ERP can remain the financial system of record while a CRM, partner portal, or payment service accesses selected capabilities through controlled interfaces.

The practical challenge is keeping those connections correct when records disagree, endpoints slow down, or only part of a workflow succeeds. A new API does not resolve those problems by itself. The design needs data ownership, stable contracts, explicit failure states, and a rollout plan.

This guide explains how to make those decisions. The worked example is hypothetical, not an NMIT customer case study. For the commercial scope behind this work, see NMIT’s API integration and cloud services.

1. Decide whether to integrate or replace

Begin with the business capability you need, rather than a technology preference. Perhaps a partner needs order status, or an account team needs customer balances in the CRM. Neither requirement automatically means replacing the ERP.

Integration is worth evaluating when the existing application still performs its core job and has a supported way to expose the required data or operation. It can preserve working business rules while giving newer applications a narrower, documented interface.

Replacement deserves closer consideration when the application cannot meet essential requirements, has no viable supported interface, or creates unacceptable security and maintenance risks. An adapter can translate a protocol; it cannot restore vendor support or correct broken accounting logic.

Choose based on the constraint you need to remove
SituationDirection to evaluate
Core workflow works; another application needs accessA narrow API or adapter boundary
One capability needs change; the rest remains usefulIncremental modernization with coexistence
Data definitions are inconsistentOwnership and mapping before additional connections
The application cannot meet essential operating requirementsReplacement or retirement, with an integration transition plan

For incremental replacement, the AWS Strangler Fig guidance (opens in a new tab) describes coexistence between old and new functionality. Its limitations matter: traffic must be routable, the intermediary can become a bottleneck, and each migrated capability needs a rollback plan.

2. Map the current landscape before designing a new layer

Inventory the interfaces involved in one business flow. Record the application owner, consuming team, protocol, data exchanged, expected frequency, and consequence of failure. A diagram showing only application names leaves out the decisions that determine delivery scope.

Ask about end-of-day jobs, month-end processing, maintenance windows, and manual corrections. A flow that looks healthy during an ordinary test may behave differently during a scheduled batch run.

Hypothetical inventory for a partner-onboarding flow
InterfaceOwnership to establishBehavior to verify
CRM → customer registrationCustomer operations and integration engineeringDuplicate requests and rejected records
ERP → account statusFinance and ERP supportFreshness, access rules, and maintenance windows
Integration → partner endpointPartner operations and delivery engineeringTimeouts, rate limits, and status lookup
ERP → reconciliation reportFinance operationsMissing records and correction approval

Prefer documented APIs, supported messaging, or approved file interfaces. If direct database access is considered, establish vendor support, access boundaries, and schema-change responsibilities first. Treat undocumented writes to an application database as a separate risk decision.

3. Choose APIs, events, or batch for each workflow

A business landscape often needs more than one integration pattern. Match the pattern to the required response, data freshness, and failure tolerance.

For a deeper comparison of latency, coupling, ordering, and operating cost, use our API vs event-driven vs batch integration decision guide.

Three patterns and the operating questions they create
PatternUseful whenPlan for
Request–response APIA caller needs a result before proceedingTimeouts, downstream availability, and load limits
Events or queued messagesWork can continue asynchronously or reach several consumersDuplicates, ordering, replay, and delayed consistency
Scheduled batch or file exchangeThe business accepts a defined delayMissing files, partial processing, and reconciliation

For example, a customer eligibility check may require an immediate API response. Updating a reporting copy may tolerate asynchronous events. A daily settlement comparison may be better suited to a controlled batch job.

Asynchronous design adds its own responsibilities. Microsoft’s event-driven architecture guidance (opens in a new tab) discusses delivery, ordering, eventual consistency, and recovery challenges. A queue should not be presented as an automatic guarantee that every business operation completes once.

Keep protocol translation near the system it serves. Microsoft calls this an anti-corruption layer (opens in a new tab): a boundary between systems with different semantics. It can be an application component or a separate service. The added latency and operating burden still need evaluation.

A shared integration architecture describes agreed contracts and responsibilities. It does not require one central server or a microservice for every connection.

4. Define data ownership and contracts before mapping fields

Our ERP–CRM data mapping, synchronization, and error-handling guide works through stable keys, field authority, conflicting updates, and failed-record recovery.

Decide which application owns each fact. The CRM might own relationship notes, while the ERP owns an approved account status. Allowing both systems to overwrite the same field without a conflict rule makes synchronization unpredictable.

Then define identity mappings. In this fictional example, the ERP’s CUST_NO and the CRM’s contact_id refer to related records but are different identifiers. A contract exposes a stable customerId, with a maintained cross-reference to each system. Renaming a field is insufficient if records do not have a reliable identity relationship.

For each interface, document required fields, allowed values, formats, null handling, error responses, pagination, and version compatibility. For HTTP APIs, the OpenAPI Specification (opens in a new tab) provides a standard way to describe the interface. A specification documents the contract; implementation tests must still verify that the service follows it.

Agree how changes will be introduced. Adding an optional field is different from changing an identifier’s meaning. Identify consumers, set a notice period, and test supported versions before retiring an old contract.

5. Design for partial failure, not just successful calls

A successful workflow in a test environment proves only one path. Define what happens when a dependency responds slowly, accepts a request but loses the response, or rejects one record in a larger batch.

A timeout means the caller stopped waiting. It does not, by itself, establish whether the remote operation completed. Where the outcome is unknown, preserve a pending or unresolved state and use the partner’s documented status or reconciliation mechanism.

  • Retries: identify which failures are retryable, cap attempts, and avoid overwhelming a recovering dependency.
  • Idempotency: use a stable operation identifier where the receiving interface supports it, and verify its scope and retention behavior.
  • Failed messages: quarantine records with a reason and a controlled recovery process.
  • Reconciliation: compare business records across systems and assign an owner to unresolved differences.

Stripe’s idempotent request documentation (opens in a new tab) is a useful concrete example: repeated requests with the same key can return a saved result, subject to documented conditions. Those semantics belong to Stripe’s interface. They should not be assumed for every partner, and idempotency alone does not guarantee end-to-end settlement correctness.

For a closer look at the payment-specific decisions, read payment API integration: timeouts, retries, and reconciliation. Apply the same discipline to account creation and other operations with external side effects.

6. Secure each boundary and limit what it exposes

Authenticate the caller, authorize the requested operation, and check access to the specific record. An authenticated partner should not be able to retrieve another partner’s customer by changing an identifier.

OWASP’s object-level authorization guidance (opens in a new tab) explains this distinction. Include negative authorization tests, rather than testing only requests with valid credentials.

Expose only the fields needed for the workflow. Agree credential storage and rotation, network restrictions, encrypted transport, audit retention, and access to operational tools. Avoid placing secrets or unnecessary personal data in logs. Existing systems and new interfaces both belong in the threat review.

Industry or jurisdiction-specific controls need a separate assessment. Connecting a banking system through an API does not establish regulatory compliance.

7. A worked example: ERP, CRM, and a partner onboarding service

Consider a fictional organization with customer relationship records in a CRM, approved account records in an ERP, and an external partner that registers eligible customers. The ERP remains in place; only this onboarding flow is changed.

  1. The CRM requests onboarding using a business operation ID and a customer reference.
  2. A contract boundary validates the request and resolves the CRM-to-ERP identity mapping.
  3. An ERP adapter reads the approved account status through a supported interface.
  4. The integration calls the partner using the partner’s documented duplicate-prevention mechanism, if available.
  5. The workflow records a confirmed, rejected, or unresolved result. It updates the CRM only with a state justified by evidence.
  6. An operations process investigates overdue unresolved requests and compares partner records with internal records.

Suppose the partner accepts the request but the response is lost. The CRM should not immediately show a confirmed registration, and a new blind submission could duplicate the operation. The recovery path depends on the partner’s contract: query status, process an authenticated callback, reconcile records, or escalate for manual investigation.

The boundary to keep clear

The illustration and workflow are design examples. They do not describe a deployed NMIT product, a customer implementation, or a guaranteed result.

The useful outcome is an explicit responsibility map: the ERP retains account authority, the CRM owns the customer-facing view, and the integration owner handles cross-system states. Discuss the relevant boundaries through NMIT’s integration-modernization workshop enquiry.

8. Roll out one bounded workflow before expanding

Choose a pilot with understandable dependencies and a measurable business outcome. Record the existing behavior, agree acceptance tests, and identify the team that can stop or reverse the rollout.

Map and test

Use representative records, unusual field values, permission failures, and dependency outages. Verify contract behavior as well as business results. Where possible, compare read-only outputs before routing production requests through the new path.

Pilot with a defined rollback gate

Limit the initial scope to an agreed group or workflow. Track errors, unresolved records, and downstream load. Define who authorizes rollback and how in-flight work will be reconciled. Switching traffic back does not undo an external side effect.

Expand and retire redundant paths

Increase scope only after the receiving team accepts the pilot. Remove superseded connections deliberately, with documentation and a recovery plan. Keeping both write paths active indefinitely can produce conflicts and hide which application owns an update.

If the rollout also changes hosting, bring the dependency inventory into cloud migration and infrastructure planning. Application connectivity, identity, and scheduled processing still need attention after a workload moves.

9. Monitor the business workflow and name its owner

Technical monitoring should tell you where a request failed. Business monitoring should tell you whether the intended operation reached a justified final state. An endpoint can be available while onboarding records remain unresolved.

OpenTelemetry’s signal documentation (opens in a new tab) describes traces, metrics, and logs. Use those signals to connect activity across boundaries, then add workflow-specific checks such as unresolved record age and reconciliation differences.

Agree alert thresholds with the owning team. Include a runbook, escalation route, credential process, deployment and rollback instructions, and a controlled method for correcting or replaying records. Business IDs used for investigation should not expose unnecessary personal data.

This operating scope belongs alongside DevOps and embedded engineering support. Specify responsibilities and support hours in the engagement; do not assume the delivery team remains the permanent incident owner.

10. A legacy integration readiness checklist

Before approving implementation, check that the team can answer each of these questions:

  • Which business capability is changing, and which systems remain?
  • Who owns each record, field, interface, and unresolved operation?
  • Are the interfaces supported and accessible in a representative test environment?
  • Are identity mapping, contracts, access rules, and version changes documented?
  • What happens after duplicates, timeouts, partial writes, and partner outages?
  • What evidence confirms success, and who reconciles conflicting records?
  • How is the pilot stopped, and how are side effects handled after rollback?
  • Can the receiving team operate, diagnose, and recover the workflow?

Unanswered questions belong in discovery scope. They should not disappear into a fixed estimate that assumes every interface behaves as expected.

Common questions about legacy system integration

Can a legacy application be integrated if it has no REST API?

Sometimes. A supported SOAP interface, message queue, file exchange, or approved data-access mechanism may provide a boundary. The choice depends on vendor support, required behavior, and acceptable delay. An adapter cannot create a safe write operation where none exists.

Do we need microservices to connect ERP and CRM?

No. A bounded adapter inside an application may be sufficient. Separate services are useful when independent deployment, scaling, or ownership justifies their operating complexity.

How long does a legacy integration project take?

There is no useful universal duration. Scope depends on interface quality, mappings, security review, test access, failure handling, and rollout constraints. Estimate after a bounded discovery exercise, with assumptions stated explicitly.

Does integration remove the need for a future replacement?

No. It can give consumers stable boundaries during a transition. The legacy application’s support status, business fit, and maintenance needs still determine whether it should eventually be replaced.

Payment API Integration: Handling Timeouts, Retries, and Reconciliation

A lost response is not proof of a failed payment. Keep uncertainty visible, prevent duplicate operations, and reconcile against independent evidence.

Published by NMITPublished 5 January 2024Updated 17 September 202611 min read
On this page
  1. Separate request and payment state
  2. A timeout, worked through
  3. Choose stable operation keys
  4. Make retries bounded
  5. Process callbacks safely
  6. Reconcile three records
  7. Protect the boundary
  8. Test the failure paths
  9. Common questions

Bring the workflow, its owners, and a clear definition of completion.

Payment API integration connects a business application with a payment provider while maintaining a trustworthy record of what was requested, what the provider confirmed, and what eventually settled. Handling timeouts, retries, and reconciliation is central to that record.

When a payment request times out, the caller knows it did not receive a complete response. It may not know whether the provider received, processed, or completed the operation. Treating that uncertainty as a decline can lead to a second charge; treating it as success can trigger premature fulfilment.

This guide expands our partner-payment article with a hypothetical order, a recovery policy, and a reconciliation process. For the wider system boundaries, begin with connecting legacy ERP, CRM, and partner systems. The states below are an application model, not a replacement for any provider’s documented lifecycle.

Keep transport state separate from payment state

A successful HTTP exchange and a successful financial operation are different facts. An accepted request may still require customer action, asynchronous processing, or later capture. Similarly, a network exception does not establish that no money moved.

Stripe’s PaymentIntent lifecycle (opens in a new tab) illustrates why an integration needs more than a paid/unpaid flag. Map provider-specific statuses into your application explicitly, preserving the original status and resource ID for investigation.

An illustrative application state model
Local stateEvidenceNext action
PreparedDurable intent exists; provider request not yet dispatchedValidate inputs, persist an operation key, dispatch once
UnknownResponse missing or outcome indeterminateResolve with documented status lookup, safe retry, or investigation
Processing / action requiredProvider confirms an intermediate stateWait or guide the customer through the required action
Confirmed failedAuthoritative provider evidence of failureShow a justified failure; apply a new-attempt policy
Confirmed succeededProvider confirms the required payment stageApply the business effect once; continue settlement checks
Reconciliation exceptionInternal and external records disagreeAssign an owner and investigate the specific mismatch

Record authorisation, capture, refund, and settlement separately when your payment method distinguishes them. A captured charge can later be refunded or disputed; those are additional operations and ledger entries, not a reason to erase the original evidence. Agree which stage permits dispatch, account activation, or partner credit.

Worked example: the provider accepted the payment, but the response was lost

Imagine order ORD-1042 for INR 1,250.00. The amount is fictional. The provider in this example supports idempotent creation with a retained operation key and a resource-status endpoint. Check those capabilities before adopting this recovery path.

  1. Before dispatch: persist operation PAY-1042-A, amount 125000 paise, currency INR, request fingerprint, and a random idempotency key. A database uniqueness rule prevents two workers from claiming the same charge intent.
  2. The request leaves: the provider creates payment resource P-778. The response is lost between the provider and your application. Your client’s illustrative five-second deadline expires.
  3. The application records Unknown: keep the original key and payload. Show “Payment confirmation pending” and prevent a second submission for the same active intent. Do not mark the order paid or tell the customer the payment definitely failed.
  4. A recovery worker resolves it: if the resource ID is known, query its status. If it is not known and the provider documents safe replay for this failure, retry the same operation with the same key and unchanged parameters within the supported retention window.
  5. Confirmation arrives: the replay returns P-778, or an authenticated callback identifies it. A conditional state transition and a unique business-effect key ensure the order is fulfilled once.
  6. Finance verifies later: compare the provider’s records with the payment operation and the internal ledger. A later refund or settlement adjustment has its own evidence and accounting treatment.

If the provider supports neither reliable status retrieval nor safe duplicate prevention, stop automatic replay after an ambiguous write. Route the operation to an investigation queue with the provider reference, timestamps, and request ID. Asking the customer to click Pay again is not a recovery strategy.

The same partial-failure reasoning appears in our legacy-integration failure-handling guide. It applies whenever a remote side effect can outlive the caller’s response window.

Make the key identify one business operation

An idempotency key lets a provider recognise a repeated operation according to its own contract. Persist it before sending the request. Scope it to the merchant account and operation type; capture, refund, and charge creation must not accidentally share one intent.

Stripe’s idempotent-request reference (opens in a new tab) documents saved responses, parameter matching, and key pruning after at least 24 hours. That window is Stripe-specific. Your internal duplicate guard should cover your own business replay window even after an external key expires.

PayPal’s idempotency guidance (opens in a new tab) uses PayPal-Request-Id, with support and retention determined by the API. Adyen’s idempotency reference (opens in a new tab) also describes provider-specific retry signals. Write a capability matrix for each endpoint instead of assuming one payment-provider abstraction gives them identical guarantees.

Use a new key only for a genuinely new operation. A changed amount requires a controlled new attempt after the earlier intent is resolved or safely cancelled. Store the request fingerprint, attempt count, last outcome, and resource reference so an operator can explain why a replay is safe.

The database still has a job

Provider idempotency does not prevent your application from fulfilling an order twice, adding duplicate ledger entries, or processing the same callback twice. Protect those local effects independently.

Classify the failure before scheduling a retry

Define connection, read, and total deadlines. Choose them from measured provider latency and the customer’s acceptable wait, not from an arbitrary long timeout. Account for retry behavior already built into the SDK: an application retry wrapped around SDK retries can multiply requests.

Recovery decisions depend on endpoint semantics
FailureDefault integration responseCondition to verify
Validation or authentication errorCorrect input or credentials; do not blindly retryWhether the endpoint began execution
Read timeout / connection lost after dispatchMark outcome unknownStatus lookup or documented replay with the original key
Rate limitedPause; honour documented retry timingQuota scope, retry signal, and operation safety
Server errorPreserve uncertainty about side effectsProvider guidance; a new key may duplicate an operation
Confirmed business declineShow the documented resultWhether a new customer-authorised attempt is appropriate

Stripe’s advanced error handling (opens in a new tab) treats certain server errors as indeterminate and warns against retrying with a new key. A repeated cached error is not evidence that the original request had no side effects. Follow the endpoint’s documented recovery behavior.

A proposed background policy might use capped exponential delay with jitter, a maximum attempt count, and an overall resolution deadline. These are design parameters to test. Stop automatic retries when safety cannot be established, and escalate overdue unknowns rather than deleting them.

HTTP’s Retry-After definition (opens in a new tab) explains the header’s timing formats. Do not retry earlier than a valid provider instruction. A circuit breaker (opens in a new tab) can reduce calls to an unhealthy dependency, but opening it does not resolve operations already sent.

Treat callbacks as evidence that needs validation

Verify the provider’s signature using the required original payload and secret. Persist the accepted event durably before acknowledging delivery, then process it asynchronously. If durable acceptance fails, return an appropriate failure so the sender can follow its delivery policy.

Stripe’s webhook documentation (opens in a new tab) covers signature verification, duplicate events, and delivery without guaranteed order. Deduplicate by the documented event identity, then separately guard business effects: multiple different events can refer to one payment.

A late processing notification must not overwrite a later confirmed capture. Apply valid lifecycle transitions; retrieve the current provider resource when event order leaves the state unclear. Keep refunds and disputes distinct from the charge’s success state. This is a useful application of the API and event-driven integration tradeoffs.

Reconcile the operation, the provider record, and the ledger

Reconciliation checks whether independent records describe the same financial activity. Confirmation of one charge does not prove that fees, refunds, settlement, and bank deposits all match. Build an exception process alongside the matching job.

Match by merchant account, provider resource ID, internal operation ID, amount, and currency. Retain the original transaction date and the report’s settlement date or timezone. Avoid floating-point arithmetic for monetary comparisons; use the provider’s currency-unit rules and separate currencies in totals.

Stripe’s balance transaction types (opens in a new tab) distinguish categories such as charges, refunds, fees, and adjustments. Stripe’s bank reconciliation documentation (opens in a new tab) describes reconciling cash movements with bank statements. Choose reports and reconciliation boundaries available to your own account and provider.

  • Missing internal record: investigate an external payment with no matching operation; do not silently insert a guessed order association.
  • Missing external record: distinguish reporting delay from an incorrectly confirmed local payment.
  • Amount or currency mismatch: compare the original intent, capture, partial refund, fee treatment, and exchange-rate handling.
  • Duplicate effect: check whether duplicate ledger entries represent one charge or two separate provider operations.

Set an owner, ageing threshold, and correction approval for every exception category. Re-running a report should update the same exception, not create a new unresolved ticket each day. Preserve a correction history; never erase evidence to force totals to match.

When payment results feed customer records, our ERP–CRM synchronization guide explains field ownership and failed updates. Finance retains authority for the financial record even when the CRM displays its status.

Protect credentials and make investigation possible

Keep payment credentials on the server, restrict permission by operation, and redact sensitive payloads from logs. Verify object-level access before exposing a payment status to a user. OWASP’s object-level authorisation guidance (opens in a new tab) describes the access checks that resource identifiers require.

Log correlation IDs, attempt timing, classified error, and state transitions without storing raw card data or secrets. Track the oldest unknown payment, callback-processing delay, retry volume, and reconciliation exceptions. OpenTelemetry’s signals overview (opens in a new tab) separates traces, metrics, and logs; connect those signals using the business operation reference.

These operating responsibilities should be part of the delivery scope. NMIT’s integration and DevOps services cover the application boundary and its production ownership.

Test the paths that ordinary happy-path demos miss

  • Lose the response after a simulated provider acceptance. Verify Unknown, stable keys, and no duplicate fulfilment.
  • Crash the worker before dispatch and after dispatch. Recover from durable intent without guessing whether the request left.
  • Deliver duplicate callbacks and callbacks in reverse order. Verify valid state transitions and one local effect.
  • Return throttling and prolonged server errors. Check retry caps, escalation, and customer messaging.
  • Re-run the same settlement file, omit a record, and introduce a partial refund. Check exception deduplication and accounting ownership.
  • Attempt status access from another customer account. Confirm authorisation and log redaction.

For scenario setup and observable pass criteria, use our payment API testing checklist.

Use sandbox facilities and fault injection before a controlled production pilot. Document which provider guarantees were verified and which behaviors were only simulated. Bring unresolved recovery questions to an integration workshop with NMIT.

Common questions about payment API integration

Should every timed-out payment be retried?

No. Retry a write only when the provider’s duplicate-prevention and failure semantics make replay safe. Otherwise resolve its status or investigate it. A timeout alone is not a decline.

Does an idempotency key guarantee exactly-once payment handling?

It addresses repeated provider requests within a documented scope and retention window. Your state store, ledger, callback worker, and fulfilment process still need their own duplicate protection.

Can webhooks replace reconciliation?

No. Webhooks help update operational state. Reconciliation compares independent financial records and catches missing entries, fees, settlement differences, and adjustments.

Plan your integration

Give the workflow a clear operating plan.
